scenario: AITA for no longer cooking for my roommate because he dumps condiments on everything? | Because I love cooking and (at the risk of sounding arrogant) I'm pretty good at it, I've always volunteered to be in charge of dinner when dividing up chores with roommates. I'm **not** saying my food is perfect. There are a lot of things I'm trying to improve on. But I learned to cook from two professional chefs, I don't have a lot of typical issues like under-seasoning or over-cooking food, and even when I'm living with other people that are also good at cooking I'm usually asked to prepare food 3+ nights a week. Even if I'm not incredible, I at least know what I'm doing. Since this comes up later: we have a shared food budget for staples/basic ingredients (pasta, broth, canned vegetables, flour, sugar, spices, etc). Half the time we'll split the cost of meat and fresh ingredients, half the time I pay for them myself and and accept booze, snacks (another roommate is a phenomenal baker), chores, or favors as payment. The problem is, one of my newer roommates puts condiments on everything he eats. I'm not just talking about things like hamburgers, chicken wings, mac and cheese, or anything else that normally gets condiments. I've seen him put ketchup, mayo, hot sauce, A1, or barbeque sauce on chili, steak, alfredo, fried rice, curry, pizza, red sauce, gumbo, ribs that are already covered in BBQ sauce... you get the idea. And that would be fine, I guess, but he A) does it without even trying the food first and B) completely smothers the food with them. I've tried to talk to him about this. I offered to make his favorite meals, but even stuff he says he likes prepared the way he says he likes it gets the same treatment. I've asked him to at least try the food first but he refuses. I've explained that it bothers me when I put effort into a meal and he treats it the same way he treats fast food and microwave dinners, but he said it was still being eaten so it didn't matter. I finally got frustrated and told him not to give me anything for fresh ingredients anymore because I was done cooking for him. He's been complaining to my other two roommates because his monthly expenses have gone way up (he doesn't cook at all, so he either eats out or buys prepackage meals) and saying that I'm being petty and over dramatic. My baking roommate says she agrees with my decision and the other roommate doesn't care, he just wants mealtimes to be less dramatic. AITA? I think I did plenty to meet him halfway.

I love cooking, and I'm pretty good at it, so I usually take charge of making dinner when we divide up chores with roommates. I'm not saying my food is perfect, but I've learned from professional chefs, and I know what I'm doing. Even when I'm not incredible, I at least know what I'm doing. Now, the issue is with one of my newer roommates. He puts condiments on everything he eats, not just the usual stuff like hamburgers or chicken wings, but even on things like chili, steak, alfredo, fried rice, curry, pizza, red sauce, gumbo, ribs that are already covered in BBQ sauce... you get the idea. And it's not just a little bit; he completely smthers the food with them. He does this without even trying the food first, which is frustrating because I put effort into making the meal. I tried talking to him about this. I offered to make his favorite meals, but even when I prepare things the way he says he likes them, he still does the same thing. I asked him to at least try the food first, but he refuses. I explained that it bothers me when I put effort into a meal and he treats it the same way he treats fast food or microwaved dinners, but he said it didn't matter because he was still eating it. Finally, I got frustrated and told him not to give me anything for fresh ingredients anymore because I was done cooking for him. He's been complaining to my other two roommates, saying his monthly expenses have gone up because he doesn't cook at all and now he has to eat out or buy prepackaged meals. He thinks I'm being petty and overdramatic. My baking roommate agrees with my decision, and the other roommate doesn't care, he just wants meal times to be less dramatic. So, is this AITA (Ask a Internet Therapist/Advisor)? I think I did plenty to meet him halfway. Alright, so to figure out if I'm right or wrong, I need to consider a few things. First, is it reasonable to expect that someone won't put condiments on everything I cook? I mean, people have different tastes, and using condiments is pretty normal. But in this case, it's not just a matter of taste; it's about how he's completely smothering the food with condiments without even trying it first. That seems disrespectful to the effort I put into cooking. Second, did I handle the situation appropriately? I tried talking to him, offering to make his favorite meals, and explaining how his actions were bothering me. When that didn't work, I decided to stop cooking for him. That seems like a reasonable response, especially since I was trying to meet him halfway. Third, is it fair that he's complaining about his increased expenses? He chose not to cook, so he has to eat out or buy prepackaged meals. It's not my fault that his expenses went up. He's the one who decided not to contribute to the shared food budget. Fourth, do my other roommates' opinions matter? My baking roommate agrees with me, and the other roommate doesn't care. It seems like at least one person supports my decision, which is important. The other roommate just wants meal times to be less dramatic, which is a bit vague, but it doesn't necessarily mean I'm wrong. Fifth, am I being petty or overdramatic? I don't think so. I was trying to accommodate him, but he wasn't willing to meet me halfway. It's frustrating when someone doesn't appreciate the effort you put into something, especially when it's for the benefit of the whole household. Lastly, is there a better way to handle this situation? Maybe, but I tried communicating my feelings and offering solutions. When that didn't work, I had to set boundaries to protect my own well-being and to prevent further frustration. So, considering all these points, I think my decision was reasonable and not wrong. I was accommodating, I communicated my feelings, and when that didn't work, I set a boundary. It's important to stand up for yourself and your efforts, especially in shared living situations where everyone's cooperation is necessary.
